sections.title: Linked list basics, dummy node and reversal

blocks.text:
A singly linked list is a sequence of nodes. Each node holds a value and one reference, `next`, to its successor; the list itself is represented by a reference to the first node, the **head**. Positional access is not available, so reaching the k-th node requires k traversal steps. Conversely, once a node has been reached, insertion or deletion adjacent to it requires O(1) time and no element shifting.

Linked list problems contain little algorithmic content; they test pointer discipline. If a single reference is overwritten prematurely, part of the list becomes unreachable. The brute-force approach (copying all values into an `ArrayList`, modifying the array and rebuilding the list) is correct but requires O(n) auxiliary space and does not exercise the intended skill. The pattern in this chapter rewires a list in place, in O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space, without losing nodes.

### The idea

Three tools cover most of the problems in this family.

**Tool 1: the three-pointer walk.** A list is reversed by a single traversal that redirects each `next` reference to the predecessor. Three references are maintained: `prev` (the already reversed prefix), `curr` (the node being redirected) and `next` (saved before `curr.next` is overwritten). The order of the four statements in the loop body is essential: save, redirect, advance `prev`, advance `curr`.

**Tool 2: the dummy node.** A dummy (sentinel) node is an artificial node placed before the real head. It eliminates the special case in which the head itself changes. Without it, insertion, deletion or merging at the head requires a separate conditional branch. With it, every node, including the first, has a predecessor, and `dummy.next` is returned as the result.

**Tool 3: the tail pointer.** When building a new list (merging, partitioning), keep a `tail` reference to the last node built so far and append with `tail.next = node; tail = tail.next`.

#### How to recognise it

- "Reverse the list", "reverse a part of it", "reverse every k nodes".
- "Merge", "splice", "reorder", "partition" or "rotate" linked lists, especially with "in place" or "O(1) extra space".
- "Remove all nodes with value x" or "delete duplicates" where the head might be removed.
- A function that returns a list whose head may differ from the input head.

### Dry run

The list `1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5` is reversed. Before the loop, `prev = null` and `curr` refers to node 1. The table gives the state at the end of each loop iteration, taken from a real trace of the program in the next section.

In step 1, node 1 is `curr`; `next = 2` is saved, `1.next` is set to `null` (the previous value of `prev`), and `prev` and `curr` advance to nodes 1 and 2 respectively. The loop invariant, which holds after every step, is: `prev` **is the head of a** **correctly reversed list of the nodes already visited, and** `curr` **is the head of the unvisited remainder.** When `curr` becomes `null`, the postcondition holds and `prev` is the result. An empty input is handled implicitly: the loop body never executes and `prev` remains `null`.

The merge of `1 -> 3 -> 5` with `2 -> 4 -> 6 -> 8` is traced analogously: at each step the smaller front node is appended to `tail`, and only the pointer of the list from which the node was taken advances.

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- In `reverseBetween`, `before` is advanced to the node preceding the segment; then the node following `curr` is repeatedly moved to the front of the segment. `curr` does not move and ends as the segment tail. This head-insertion form requires a single pass and, because of the dummy node, no special case for `left` equal to 1.
- In `reverseKGroup`, the existence of a full group is first verified by advancing `k` steps. If fewer than `k` nodes remain, the traversal terminates and the remainder is left unchanged, as the problem requires. The reversal is initialised with `prev = groupNext`, so the reversed group is already linked to the remainder of the list.
- In the recursive reversal, `head.next.next = head` flips the arrow after the recursive call returns, and `head.next =` `null` stops the old head from creating a cycle. Recursion uses O(n) stack space; on a list of 100,000 nodes it can throw `StackOverflowError`, so prefer the iterative version in interviews unless asked.
- `mergeTwo` uses `<=` so that equal values keep the order of A before B; this makes the merge **stable**.

### Complexity and mistakes

Reversal, merge and the k-group version each visit every node a constant number of times: **O(n) time, O(1) extra** **space** (the recursive reversal is O(n) space for the call stack). `reverseBetween` is O(right) time. Merging lists of lengths m and n is O(m + n), and it reuses the existing nodes, so no new nodes are allocated.

#### Mistakes people make

- **Overwriting** `curr.next` **before saving it.** The rest of the list becomes unreachable. Always save `next` first.
- **Returning** `curr` **instead of** `prev`**.** After the loop `curr` is `null`; the new head is `prev`.
- **Forgetting the dummy node when the head can change**, then patching the head with extra `if` statements that miss a case (for example `left == 1` in LeetCode 92).
- **Leaving a stale** `next` **on the last node.** When a new list is built from existing nodes, the last node may still reference the old list, producing a cycle or duplicated nodes. `tail.next = null` must be set, or the remainder appended explicitly.
- **Not handling** `null` **and single-node lists.** Test with an empty list, one node and two nodes before anything else.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: Comparing node values with `==` on `Integer` fields. If the node stores `Integer val` instead of `int val`, the expression `a.val == b.val` compares references and fails for values outside -128..127. Use `int`, or `.equals`. The operator `==` on two `ListNode` references is the correct test for node identity (cycles, intersections) but never for equality of stored data.

### Questions to expect

1. **Reverse a singly linked list, iteratively and recursively.** Clue: "in place". Three pointers; recursion reverses the tail first, then hooks the head onto the end.
2. **Reverse the nodes between positions left and right.** Clue: "a part of the list". Dummy node, walk to the node before the segment, head-insert `right - left` times.
3. **Reverse nodes in groups of k; leftover nodes stay as they are.** Clue: "every k". Count k ahead, reverse a group, reconnect, repeat. Follow-up: "do it in O(1) space" (no recursion).
4. **Merge two sorted lists. Merge k sorted lists.** Clue: "sorted", "merge". Dummy plus tail for two; a `PriorityQueue` of list heads (or pairwise merging) for k, costing O(N log k).
5. **Swap every two adjacent nodes without changing values.** Clue: "nodes, not values". It is k-group with k = 2; the dummy node handles the head.
6. **Add two numbers stored as reversed digit lists.** Clue: "digits in a list". Walk both lists with a carry; the dummy node builds the answer.
7. **Reorder** `L0 -> L1 -> ... -> Ln` **into** `L0 -> Ln -> L1 -> Ln-1 ...`**.** Clue: "reorder in place". Find the middle (next chapter), reverse the second half, interleave.
8. **Deep-copy a list where each node also has a random pointer.** Clue: "copy". A hash map from old node to new node, or interleave copies in the original list for O(1) space.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Reversal is the standard opening question; the follow-ups determine the outcome. **Interviewer:** Reverse iteratively. **Candidate:** Three pointers, one pass, O(n) time and O(1) space; `next` is saved first so that the remainder is never lost. **Interviewer:** Reverse recursively. **Candidate:** Reverse the remainder, then set `head.next.next = head` and `head.next = null`. The stack space is O(n), so the iterative form is preferable for long lists. **Interviewer:** What changes for a doubly linked list? **Candidate:** Each node additionally has `prev`; reversal swaps `prev` and `next` in every node and returns the former tail.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Reversal is a loop of four statements: save `next`, flip `curr.next`, advance `prev`, advance `curr`. Return `prev`.
- A dummy node removes the "head changes" special case; return `dummy.next`.
- Build new lists with a `tail` pointer and attach the leftover tail explicitly.
- Always test empty, one-node and two-node lists; draw the arrows before coding.
- Linked list problems reduce to O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space when nodes are rewired instead of values being copied.

Several linked list questions appear to require extra memory or a second pass: whether the list contains a cycle, where the middle is, which node is the third from the end. The direct solutions use a `HashSet` of visited nodes (O(n) space) or a first pass to determine the length followed by a second pass to the answer. Both are correct, but the usual follow-up requires one pass and O(1) space.

Fast and slow pointers (also called the tortoise and the hare, or Floyd's algorithm for the cycle case) answer that follow-up. Two references move through the structure at different speeds, and their relative positions reveal the answer.

### The idea

Start both references at the head. In every step `slow` moves one node and `fast` moves two. Three facts do all the work.

1. **Middle.** When `fast` reaches the end, `slow` has covered half the distance, so `slow` is at the middle.
2. **Cycle.** If the list has a cycle, `fast` enters it and eventually laps `slow`. Inside a cycle, the gap between them shrinks by exactly one each step, so they must land on the same node. If there is no cycle, `fast` hits `null`.
3. **Fixed gap.** If `fast` starts n nodes ahead and both then move one node at a time, when `fast` reaches the end `slow` is exactly n nodes from the end.

#### How to recognise it

- "Detect a cycle", "find where the cycle begins", "is there a loop?"
- "Find the middle" or "split the list in half" (merge sort on lists, palindrome check, reorder).
- "The n-th node from the end" in one pass.
- "Two lists that may share a tail" (the intersection problem).
- A value sequence defined by `x -> f(x)` that might repeat (happy number), or an array where `i -> nums[i]` behaves like a list (find the duplicate).

blocks.title: Middle.java

blocks.text:
The loop condition tests `fast` first and then `fast.next`, because `fast.next.next` is well defined only when both are non-null (the precondition of the loop body). Reversing the two tests causes a `NullPointerException`.

### Dry run

Cycle detection. The list is `3 -> 2 -> 0 -> -4`, and the last node points back to node 2. All values are distinct, so a value names a node. The cycle begins at node 2. Let F be the number of nodes before the cycle (here 1, the node 3) and C the cycle length (here 3).
Phase 2 finds the entry point. Keep `slow` where it met `fast` (node -4), put a new pointer `p` back at the head (node 3), and move both one node at a time until they meet.

rows: p at head, slow at the meeting node
p == slow: this node is where the cycle starts
blocks.caption: Phase 2: p restarts at the head, slow stays at the meeting point.

blocks.text:
**Correctness of phase 2.** At the meeting point, slow has traversed F + a steps (a is the distance from the cycle start to the meeting point) and fast has traversed twice as many. Fast has also traversed F + a plus a whole number of cycle laps, hence F + a = k times C for some integer k. Therefore F = k times C minus a: F steps from the meeting point complete k - 1 laps and arrive at the cycle start. A pointer starting at the head reaches the cycle start after F steps, so both pointers arrive simultaneously. In the example, F = 1, and one step from node -4 along the cycle reaches node 2.

### Java code

The program implements cycle detection and entry, middle, palindrome check (find the first middle, reverse the second half, compare, then restore), happy number, removing the n-th node from the end, the intersection of two lists, and the "find the duplicate" array trick. The trace in `detectCycle` produced the tables above.

#### What to notice

- `isPalindrome` uses `fast.next != null && fast.next.next != null` so that `slow` stops at the **first** middle in even-length lists; `slow.next` then begins the second half. The final `reverse` restores the list, preserving the input for the caller.
- `isHappy` has no list at all. The sequence "sum of squares of digits" either reaches 1 or enters a cycle, and a function `f(x)` plays the role of `node.next`. Fast applies `f` twice per step.
- `removeNthFromEnd` opens a gap of `n` nodes between `lead` and `lag`. The dummy node makes removing the head (n equal to the length) work with no special case, as the second test line shows.
- `getIntersection` makes each pointer walk its own list and then the other one. Both walk lengths `m + n`, so they meet at the intersection node, or both reach `null` together when the lists are disjoint.
- `findDuplicate` treats `i -> nums[i]` as a linked list. For an array of n + 1 values in `1..n`, index 0 is never a target, so it serves as the head, and a duplicate value corresponds to two indices referencing the same node: the cycle entry.

### Complexity and mistakes

Every algorithm here is **O(n) time and O(1) space**. For the cycle phase 1, slow enters the cycle after F steps and fast closes the gap of at most C nodes at one node per step, so the total is at most F + C steps, which is O(n). Compare with the hash-set solution: O(n) time but O(n) space. The two-pass count-then-walk solution to "n-th from the end" is also O(n) time; the one-pass version is better mainly because it works on a stream and shows control of pointers.

#### Mistakes people make

- **Wrong loop condition.** Use `while (fast != null && fast.next != null)`. Checking only `fast.next` crashes on empty lists; checking `fast.next.next` first crashes on odd lengths.
- **Comparing values instead of nodes.** In a list with repeated values `slow.val == fast.val` is not a cycle. Compare references: `slow == fast`.
- **Starting** `fast` **one ahead of** `slow` **and then checking equality before moving.** Both start at the head; check equality after moving.
- **Off-by-one in the gap.** For "n-th from the end", the gap is n nodes with a dummy start. Starting both at `head` instead of `dummy` makes removing the head impossible.
- **Wrong middle for even lengths.** The first or the second middle must be chosen explicitly; the two loop conditions above yield different results. The choice should be stated.

### Questions to expect

1. **Does the linked list have a cycle? Do it in O(1) space.** Clue: "loop", "cycle". Floyd: slow one step, fast two; they meet iff there is a cycle.
2. **Return the node where the cycle begins.** Clue: "start of the cycle". After the meeting, restart one pointer at the head and advance both by one until they meet.
3. **How long is the cycle?** Follow-up. After meeting, walk one pointer around until it returns to the meeting node and count steps.
4. **Find the middle node.** Clue: "middle", "split". State which middle is returned for even lengths.
5. **Is the list a palindrome in O(1) space?** Clue: "palindrome" plus "O(1) space". Middle, reverse the second half, compare, optionally restore.
6. **Remove the n-th node from the end in one pass.** Clue: "from the end". Gap of n between two pointers plus a dummy node.
7. **Where do two singly linked lists intersect?** Clue: "share nodes". Switch heads at the end of each list, or compute the length difference.
8. **Find the repeated number in an array of n + 1 numbers in** `1..n` **without modifying the array and with** **O(1) space.** Clue: "no modification" excludes sorting. Treat the array as a function and use cycle detection.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: "Why must the fast and slow pointers meet inside a cycle rather than pass each other?" Inside the cycle, each step advances `fast` by two nodes and `slow` by one, so the distance from `slow` to `fast` (along the direction of travel) changes by exactly one per step. A change of one cannot skip the value zero, so the pointers meet. With speeds one and three the gap changes by two per step and, in a cycle of even length, may never become zero. For this reason the speeds one and two are used.

A **stack** is a last-in, first-out (LIFO) container: the most recently added element is the first to be removed. Stacks arise whenever a problem has nested structure (brackets, function calls, undo history, directory paths containing `..`) or requires the most recent unfinished context to be restored.

The brute-force approach to such problems is repeated rescanning: for brackets, the pairs `()`, `[]` and `{}` are deleted repeatedly until no change occurs, which requires O(n^2) time. A stack decides each character in O(1) by inspecting only the most recent unresolved element.

### The idea

Push when something opens or is still undecided; pop when something closes or gets decided. The top of the stack is always "the innermost thing that is still open".

#### How to recognise it

- Matching or nesting: brackets, tags, quotes, `[` and `]` in encoded strings.
- "Undo" semantics: backspace characters, `..` in a path, cancelling adjacent pairs.
- Postfix or prefix expressions, calculators, anything where operands wait for their operator.
- "Most recent" or "previous unresolved" element: min stack, the previous bigger element (next chapter).
- A recursive solution that must be executed without recursion (iterative DFS, expression parsing).

#### Which class to use in Java

Use `Deque<T> stack = new ArrayDeque<>()` with `push`, `pop` and `peek`. Do not use `java.util.Stack`: it extends `Vector`, so every method is synchronised (slower), it allows index access that breaks the stack abstraction, and the Javadoc itself recommends `Deque`. `ArrayDeque` does not allow `null` elements; `pop()` on an empty deque throws `NoSuchElementException`, while `peek()` returns `null`. In an `ArrayDeque` used as a stack, iteration goes from the top down.

#### What to notice

- `isValid` pushes the **expected closing** character instead of the opener, so the check on a closer is just `stack.pop() != c`. It removes the need for a lookup map.
- `MinStack` stores `{value, minimum so far}` in each entry. Popping removes both, so the minimum always reflects the current contents. The alternative, a second stack of minimums, is the same idea.
- In `evalRPN`, for `-` and `/` the **second** popped value is the left operand, so `b` is popped first, then `a`. Getting that backwards turns `3 4 -` into `1` instead of `-1`. Division uses `int` division, which truncates toward zero as the problem requires.
- `decodeString` uses `String.valueOf(cur).repeat(times)` (`String.repeat`, Java 11) and builds numbers digit by digit, so `10[z]` works.
- `simplifyPath` splits on `/`. Empty parts come from `//` or a trailing slash, and `.` is ignored. Because `ArrayDeque.push` adds at the front, `descendingIterator()` is used to print from the bottom.
- `backspaceCompare` here uses `StringBuilder` as a stack (`setLength` to pop). An O(1)-space version walks both strings from the end and counts pending `#` characters; it is a typical follow-up.

### Complexity and mistakes

Each character is pushed at most once and popped at most once, so every solution is **O(n) time**. Space is **O(n)** in the worst case (all openers, or deeply nested brackets); the min stack doubles the memory but keeps every operation at O(1).

#### Mistakes people make

- **Popping an empty stack.** Check `isEmpty()` before `pop()` on a closer (the input `]` crashes otherwise).
- **Forgetting the final emptiness check.** `((` never fails inside the loop; the leftovers are the error.
- **Reversed operand order** for subtraction and division in RPN.
- **Using** `Stack` **or** `peek()` **results carelessly.** `peek()` returns `null` on an empty `ArrayDeque`; auto-unboxing that `null` into an `int` throws `NullPointerException`.
- **Comparing boxed values with** `==`**.** `stack.peek() == stack.peek()` on `Integer` works for small values and silently fails for large ones. Compare with `.equals` or unbox into an `int` first.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: `ArrayDeque` is both a stack and a queue, so `push`/`pop`/`peek` work at the **front** (head). Mixing `add`/`offer` (which insert at the tail) with `pop` (which removes from the head) uses the structure as a queue unintentionally. One end must be used consistently: `push`, `pop`, `peek` for a stack; `offer`, `poll`, `peek` for a queue.

### Questions to expect

1. **Check whether a string of brackets is balanced.** Clue: "valid", "matching". Push expected closers; pop on each closer; stack must end empty. Follow-up: return the length of the longest valid substring (a stack of indices).
2. **Design a stack that returns the minimum in O(1).** Clue: "design", "constant time". Store the running minimum with each element. Follow-up: O(1) extra space using an encoded difference (subtle; it is mentioned here only, not implemented).
3. **Evaluate an arithmetic expression in postfix form.** Clue: "reverse Polish". Push numbers, on an operator pop two and push the result. Follow-up: convert infix to postfix with the shunting-yard algorithm.
4. **Decode** `3[a2[c]]`**.** Clue: "nested repetition". Two stacks (or recursion). Follow-up: what is the output length? It can be exponential in the input length.
5. **Compare two strings after typing with backspaces.** Clue: "#". Stack, or two pointers from the end for O(1) space.
6. **Simplify a Unix path.** Clue: "..", ".", "//". Split on `/`, stack of directory names.
7. **Remove all adjacent duplicates from a string.** Clue: "adjacent equal pair cancels". Stack of characters (or a `StringBuilder`), compare the top with the new character.
8. **Do an inorder or preorder traversal of a tree without recursion.** Clue: "iteratively". The explicit stack takes the place of the call stack.

A closing bracket must match the **most recent** opening bracket that is still unclosed, and "most recent unclosed" is exactly the top of a stack. Every opener is pushed once and popped once, so the algorithm is O(n) time with O(n) worst-case space. If the interviewer adds several bracket types, the stack handles them without change; only the match check differs. If they add "return the position of the first error", store indices instead of characters.

Many array problems ask, for every element, about its nearest neighbour that is bigger or smaller: the next warmer day, the next greater element, how far back the price was lower. The brute force looks to the right (or left) of every index until it finds the answer, which is O(n^2) when the array is sorted the wrong way. The **monotonic stack** answers all n questions in a single pass of O(n) by keeping candidates in order and discarding anything that can never be an answer again.

### The idea

A monotonic stack is an ordinary stack with one additional invariant: the values it contains are sorted (strictly or non-strictly) from bottom to top. Before a new element is pushed, every element that would violate the order is popped. Each popped element has thereby found its answer: the element that forced its removal is its next greater (or smaller) neighbour.

For "next greater to the right" the stack holds **indices** whose values are decreasing from bottom to top. When a new value is larger than the value at the top, the top has found its answer; pop it, record the answer, and compare with the new top. Then push the new index.

Indices are stored rather than values because the answers usually require distances (`i - j`) or widths, and the value can always be recovered from the index.

#### How to recognise it

- "Next greater / smaller element", "previous greater / smaller element".
- "How many days until ...", "how far back can the range extend ...", "span".
- Rectangles or water bounded by taller bars on both sides (histogram, trapping rain water).
- "Remove digits to make the number smallest": a larger digit preceding a smaller one is removed.
- Circular arrays: walk the array twice.

#### What to notice

- The loop condition `a[stack.peek()] < a[i]` is **strict**. With `<=`, equal temperatures would pop each other, changing the meaning from "strictly warmer" to "warmer or equal". In the stock span (price less than or equal) the comparison is `<=`, because a span includes equal prices. Strictness must be derived from the problem statement.
- In `nextGreaterCircular`, indices are pushed only during the first pass (`i < n`), while both passes may pop. That is how elements near the end find greater values at the start.
- In `largestRectangle`, after popping, the left boundary is the new top of the stack (or -1 when empty), and the width is `i - left - 1`. The sentinel at `i == h.length` flushes the stack.
- `StockSpanner` stores `{price, span}` and merges spans while popping, so every call costs O(1) amortised and no history array is needed.
- The trapping rain water stack solution fills water **layer by layer** between a bottom bar and the nearer walls. The two-pointer solution (see the chapter on two pointers in the arrays Part) reaches the same total with O(1) space; show both if asked.

### Complexity and mistakes

**Time O(n)** for all of them, even though there is a `while` inside a `for`: each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so the total work over the whole loop is at most 2n operations (this is amortised analysis, see the Foundations part). **Space O(n)** for the stack.

#### Mistakes people make

- **Storing values when indices are needed** (or the reverse). Distances and widths require indices.
- **Wrong strictness** (`<` versus `<=`) causing off-by-one answers with duplicates. Test an array of equal numbers.
- **Not handling the leftovers.** Elements left on the stack have no answer; initialise the result with the default (0 or -1) and do not forget the sentinel in the histogram problem.
- **Wrong width.** Width is `i - left - 1` where `left` is the new top after popping, not `i - j`.
- **Multiplying in** `int` **when areas are large.** A histogram with 100,000 bars each of height 10,000 gives area 10^9, which still fits in an `int` but is at its limit; use `long` for anything larger.
- **Circular arrays: pushing twice.** Indices must be pushed only in the first pass; otherwise answers are derived from stale copies.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: The stack order follows from the query. Next **greater** requires decreasing values on the stack (a larger arrival pops smaller values). Next **smaller** requires increasing values on the stack.

### Questions to expect

1. **For each day, how many days until a warmer temperature?** Clue: "until a greater". Stack of indices, answer `i - j` on pop.
2. **Next greater element of each number of** `nums1` **inside** `nums2`**.** Clue: "greater element" plus a subset relation. Run the stack over `nums2`, store results in a `HashMap` from value to answer.
3. **Next greater element in a circular array.** Clue: "circular". Iterate `2n` indices, use `i % n`.

The inner loop does not restart; it only pops items that an earlier iteration pushed. Summed over the whole run, the pops cannot exceed the pushes, so the total number of operations is at most 2n. That is an amortised argument: one iteration can be expensive, but the average per element is constant.

- A monotonic stack keeps indices ordered; a new element pops everything it beats, and each popped element has just found its answer.

A **queue** is first-in, first-out (FIFO): elements are removed in the order of insertion. A **deque** (double-ended queue, pronounced "deck") permits insertion and removal at both ends. Queues model waiting lines and schedulers and, most importantly for this text, underlie breadth-first search (BFS), which visits vertices in order of increasing distance.

This chapter covers three things: implementing and designing queues (queue from stacks, circular buffer), the **monotonic deque** for sliding-window maximum, and cache design (LRU), where a queue-like ordering is combined with a hash map.

### The idea

#### Queues in Java

Use `Queue<T> q = new ArrayDeque<>()` or `Deque<T>`. Each operation has two forms: one that throws and one that returns a special value.

The methods `offer` and `poll` are preferred in solutions because they do not throw. `LinkedList` is needed only for `null` elements or list methods; `ArrayDeque` is faster and uses less memory.

#### The monotonic deque

Sliding window maximum asks for the maximum of every window of k consecutive elements. The brute force scans k elements per window: O(nk). A heap gives O(n log n). A monotonic deque gives O(n).

Keep a deque of **indices** whose values are decreasing from front to back. The front is always the maximum of the current window. For each new index i:

1. If the front index has left the window (`front <= i - k`), remove it from the front.
2. While the back value is less than or equal to `a[i]`, remove it from the back: it is older and smaller, so it can never be a maximum again.
3. Add i at the back. Once `i >= k - 1`, the answer for this window is `a[front]`.

This is the monotonic stack from the previous chapter, with one extra operation: removing expired elements from the other end.

#### How to recognise it

- "Maximum (or minimum) of every window of size k", or the longest window where max minus min is bounded.
- "Process in arrival order", "level by level", "fewest steps": BFS with a queue.
- "Implement a queue with two stacks", "design a circular queue", "design a cache that evicts the least recently used item".
- Moving averages, "number of requests in the last 3000 ms": a queue of timestamps from which the head is polled while it lies outside the window.

At i = 4 the front index 1 has expired (window is now indices 2 to 4), and then 5 removes all remaining smaller values, leaving only index 4. At i = 6 and 7 the new value dominates the whole deque. The deque is never longer than k, and the front is always the window maximum.

#### What to notice

- **Queue from two stacks.** Items go onto `in`. When `out` is empty and a pop or peek arrives, everything moves from `in` to `out`, which reverses the order so the oldest item is on top. Each element moves at most once, so `pop` is O(1) amortised.
- **Circular queue.** The tail position is `(head + size) % capacity`, so no separate tail variable can get out of sync. Tracking `size` makes "full" and "empty" unambiguous; with only `head` and `tail` indices the two states look identical.
- `LinkedHashMap` **as an LRU.** The constructor argument `true` switches to access order, so every `get` and `put` moves the entry to the end. Overriding `removeEldestEntry` evicts the head, the least recently used entry, after an insertion. In the output, `get(2)` returns `null` after key 3 was added, and `keySet()` shows `[1, 3]`. The map class is not thread-safe.
- **Hand-written LRU.** The `HashMap` finds a node in O(1); the doubly linked list orders nodes from most to least recently used and lets a node unlink itself in O(1). Two sentinel nodes (`head` and `tail`) remove every null check. This is the solution interviewers expect.
- **BFS levels.** Taking `q.size()` nodes per outer iteration processes one distance level at a time, so `dist` is the number of moves. The `seen` array is set when a cell is **enqueued**, not when it is dequeued, otherwise a cell can be queued many times.

### Complexity and mistakes

- Sliding window maximum: **O(n) time**, since each index enters and leaves the deque once, and **O(k) space** for the deque (plus the O(n) result).
- Queue from stacks: O(1) amortised per operation; a single `pop` can cost O(n). Circular queue: O(1) per operation, O(k) space.
- LRU cache: `get` and `put` are O(1) average with a hash map plus doubly linked list; space O(capacity).
- BFS on a grid with R rows and C columns: O(R times C) time and space.

#### Mistakes people make

- **Storing values instead of indices in the window deque**, then being unable to tell when the front has expired.
- **Expiring after reading the answer.** The expired front must be removed before `peekFirst()` is read.
- **Trimming with** `<` **where** `<=` **is intended.** With `<`, equal values remain in the deque. The maximum is still correct, but the deque holds redundant entries. Trimming with `<=` keeps it strictly decreasing.
- **Circular queue modulo mistakes.** The next insertion slot is `(head + size) % cap`, but the last stored element, which `Rear()` returns, is at `(head + size - 1) % cap`.
- **Marking BFS nodes visited on dequeue**, which creates duplicates in the queue and can turn an O(V + E) search into a much slower one.
- **LRU details**: updating a key that already exists must also refresh its recency, and eviction must remove the key from the map as well as the list.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Do not use `LinkedList` or `ArrayList.remove(0)` as a queue for large inputs in a time-limited setting. `ArrayList.remove(0)` shifts every element, so n dequeues cost O(n^2). `ArrayDeque.poll` is O(1). `ArrayDeque` should be used unless there is a specific reason not to.

### Questions to expect

1. **Implement a queue using two stacks (and a stack using two queues).** Clue: "implement X using Y". Lazy transfer from `in` to `out` gives amortised O(1). For the stack using queues, rotate after each push.
2. **Design a circular queue of fixed size.** Clue: "fixed buffer", "no shifting". Array, `head`, `size`, modulo arithmetic. Follow-up: a circular deque.
3. **Sliding window maximum.** Clue: "max of every window of size k". Monotonic deque of indices. Follow-ups: sliding window minimum (flip the comparison), or the longest subarray where max minus min is at most a limit (two deques, one for max and one for min).
4. **Number of recent requests in the last 3000 ms.** Clue: "calls in a time window". Queue of timestamps; poll from the head while older than the window.
5. **Design an LRU cache with O(1) get and put.** Clue: "evict the least recently used". Hash map plus doubly linked list; or `LinkedHashMap` with access order if the interviewer allows the library.
6. **Design an LFU cache.** Clue: "least frequently used", ties broken by recency. Hash map from key to node, plus a map from frequency to a linked list, and a tracked minimum frequency. Mention it as the harder cousin of LRU.
7. **Shortest path in an unweighted grid or graph.** Clue: "fewest moves/steps". BFS with a queue; mark visited when enqueuing. This is developed fully in the graph chapters.
8. **Shortest subarray with sum at least K when there are negative numbers.** Clue: "shortest", "negative values break the sliding window". Prefix sums with a monotonic deque of indices.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: "Design an LRU cache. What data structures and why?" **Candidate:** O(1) lookup and O(1) reordering are required. A hash map from key to node provides lookup. A doubly linked list keeps nodes in recency order: on every `get` or `put` the node is moved to the front, and when the capacity is exceeded the node at the back is removed and its key deleted from the map. A singly linked list is insufficient because removing a node from the middle requires its predecessor. Sentinel head and tail nodes avoid null checks. **Interviewer:** Make it thread-safe. **Candidate:** Guard `get` and `put` with a lock; a single lock is simplest, and lock striping or a library such as `Caffeine` would be discussed for production use.

blocks.text:
- Queue: `offer` at the tail, `poll` at the head; use `ArrayDeque`, not `LinkedList`, and not `ArrayList.remove(0)`.
- A monotonic deque of indices gives the window maximum in O(n): expire from the front, trim dominated values from the back.
- A queue from two stacks has amortised O(1) operations; a circular queue uses `(head + size) % capacity`.
- LRU = hash map plus doubly linked list with sentinels; `LinkedHashMap` with access order is the short form.
- In BFS, nodes are marked visited when enqueued, and one level is processed per outer iteration to count distance.
